title: Speech and slander (III.27–III.29)
hookLine: one sentence typed into a group chat about someone who isn't in it; Francis de Sales counts three wounds
tomorrow: why was an old apostle sitting there playing with a bird?

cards: One sentence, typed into a group chat, about someone who isn't in it. A few laughing faces pop up underneath. It feels like nothing.
Francis de Sales counts the wounded, and he gets three. The person talked about loses some of their good name. The people listening take the poison in.
And the one who typed it harms their own soul. One stroke of the tongue, three wounds.

teach.b: His chapters on speech start wider. Our words show what's in the heart, Francis says, so he asks for speech that is clean, modest and respectful toward everyone. Then the step before slander: judging.
He points to Christ's words in the Douay-Rheims: "Judge not, that you may not be judged." Rash judgment sees one act and pins a whole label on a person.
One bad day doesn't make someone a bad person, and we rarely see the inside of another heart. Then slander itself, with its three wounds.

teach.h: A DIG WRAPPED IN A JOKE.
teach.b: He's especially wary of slander in disguise: a dig wrapped in a joke, or criticism that opens with a compliment. And the turn toward good.
When someone is spoken ill of in front of you, excuse them if you fairly can, or gently change the subject.
Speak of the absent the way you'd want to be spoken of when you're the one not in the room.

how: Catholics count detraction and calumny, harming someone's good name, among sins against the truth, and name them in confession; the Catechism asks for interpreting others' words and deeds as favorably as possible.

o: the rules for public speaking in a church
the official penalty for lying under oath
how words can heal, or harm someone who isn't there

games.q: speech and slander — tap the pairs.
p: the absent, the listener, the speaker
excuse them, or change the subject

s: a dig wrapped in a joke doesn't really count as slander
Francis is especially wary of slander in disguise: as a joke, or opened with praise.
Francis counts three people wounded by one act of slander
the one spoken of, the ones listening, and the one speaking.
for Francis, one bad act tells you who a person really is
that's rash judgment. one act doesn't make the person, and we rarely see the heart.

games.q: at a family party, two aunts start in on a cousin who isn't there: "she always…" you're standing right there. what does Francis advise?
o: excuse her if you fairly can, or gently change the subject.
join in a little so you don't seem judgmental.
tell your cousin everything they said.
games.why: Francis's turn toward good: excuse the absent if you fairly can, or steer the talk elsewhere.

practice: Think of someone who isn't here right now, maybe someone who's annoyed you lately. Through the sit, count three true, good things about them, one finger at a time. If you pray, pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Speech and slander. Words that show the heart, and Francis's three wounds when they're turned against someone absent.

orig.note: French, the language Francis de Sales wrote in: speaking ill of someone, slander.

carryVoice: Your line: speak well, most of all about the ones who aren't in the room. Two weeks, done.
